factAnswerRaw: Version-controlled shared configuration, skills and commands, plus an onboarding path they follow
stem: A 40-person partner team wants to adopt an engineering team's Claude Code setup for their own repository, and asks how to receive it so they can become productive without repeated hand-holding. What should the originating team provide?

opts.t: A personal override skill of the same name, added to that one engineer's own configuration, leaving the team's version untouched.
Committed, version-controlled configuration, skills, and commands, together with a guided onboarding path to follow.
A recorded walkthrough of the current setup, so the partner team can watch it at their own pace.
A shared chat channel where the partner team can ask questions about the setup as they encounter them.

whyRight: The partner team needs an artifact that survives the handoff and reaches every member regardless of who attended a walkthrough or asked a question, so a version-controlled configuration with a guided onboarding path is the only option that is actually inherited rather than person-dependent.

whyWrong.A: This fits one engineer's personal variant, not a whole team's adoption; the request is for every partner-team member to receive the setup, not for one person's individual override.
whyWrong.C: A walkthrough is durable and frozen — it teaches the setup as it exists today with full confidence on the day the setup changes and the recording does not.
whyWrong.D: A chat channel is reactive support, not an inherited artifact; it depends on someone answering each time and reaches only whoever happens to ask.

t1Clause: A 40-person partner team wants to adopt an engineering team's Claude Code setup for their own repository

deepDive.principle: Section 7.1's durability axis asks whether something survives a clone and reaches someone who was not present; if not, it is not enablement. Shared, project-level configuration is version-controlled and reaches everyone who clones the repository, while anything that depends on attendance, memory, or a person answering in the moment is reactive support, not an inherited artifact.
deepDive.rightDeep: The decision table's row for this exact situation is a partner team wanting to adopt the setup; its answer is version-controlled shared configuration, skills and commands, plus an onboarding path they follow, because the artifact is inherited and nothing depends on who attended what. The stem's 40-person partner team asking to receive the setup and become productive without hand-holding is that situation directly, so this row fires regardless of team size.

wrongDeep.A: Change the request from a whole team to one engineer wanting a personal-only variant and this becomes a different row: one engineer wants their own command behaviour without affecting the team, correctly answered by a personal override skill of the same name, because personal skills override project skills of the same name and teammates are unaffected. A 40-person team-wide adoption is not that situation.
wrongDeep.C: This is the corpus's own rejected answer to the identical situation: the same partner-team adoption offered as a recorded walkthrough, rejected because it is durable and frozen — it teaches the old setup with full confidence the day the setup changes, which a live, version-controlled artifact does not do.
wrongDeep.D: Also the corpus's own rejected answer to the same situation: a shared chat channel for questions, rejected as reactive support, not an inherited artifact. It requires someone to answer each time a partner-team engineer asks, so coverage depends on who is available rather than on what was committed to the repository.

stem: A weekly code-quality analysis spanning 200 repositories at a mid-size engineering org carries no fixed deadline, but each run must dynamically fetch and inspect additional related files mid-analysis before it can reach a conclusion. Which execution mode satisfies this requirement?

opts.t: Batch API, accepting the request queue because the flexible deadline yields the standard fifty-percent cost saving.
Structured JSON output enforced by a schema, so every fetched file is captured in one parseable record.
Batch API for the main pass, followed by a separate synchronous call to fetch any files it could not retrieve.
Synchronous execution, since the run must invoke tools mid-analysis before it can conclude.

whyRight: Synchronous execution is required because the analysis must call tools mid-run to fetch and inspect additional files before concluding; the Batch API cannot execute a tool mid-request and return the result, so no deadline flexibility changes which mode the mid-analysis fetch requires.

whyWrong.A: No fixed deadline suggests Batch's cost saving, but the stem already states the run must fetch files mid-analysis, a capability Batch structurally lacks regardless of the deadline.
whyWrong.B: Structured, schema-enforced output solves how findings are parsed downstream, a different question from whether the run can execute tools mid-analysis, which this option never addresses.
whyWrong.C: A follow-up synchronous call reconstructs, after the fact, exactly what running the entire analysis synchronously from the start would have done in one step.

t1Clause: each run must dynamically fetch and inspect additional related files mid-analysis before it can reach a conclusion

deepDive.principle: Batch API trades a flexible deadline for a fixed limitation: it cannot execute a tool mid-request and return the result, and no latency SLA applies. Whether a job qualifies for Batch depends on whether it needs to call tools during the run, not on whether a human is waiting on it or how large the job is.
deepDive.rightDeep: Section 7.5's decision table addresses exactly this shape: a non-urgent analysis that fetches related files mid-analysis is still run synchronously, because Batch cannot execute a tool mid-request and return the result — the deadline is irrelevant to that limitation. The stem's 200-repository analysis has no fixed deadline but must dynamically fetch and inspect additional files before concluding, which is a mid-request tool call; that single fact fires this row regardless of scale or urgency.

wrongDeep.A: Delete the requirement that the run must fetch files mid-analysis and this becomes section 7.5's other row: an overnight tech-debt report where nobody is blocked, correctly answered by the Batch API for its 50% cost saving. The stem instead states a mid-request tool call, which that row does not have and this one does.
wrongDeep.B: This is the correct mechanism for a different row: findings that must be posted as inline PR comments, where structured JSON output enforced by a schema guarantees a parseable shape every run. That row is about how output is consumed downstream, not about whether the run can execute a tool mid-analysis, which is what this stem tests.
wrongDeep.C: Section 7.5's own REPAIR failure mode is parsing malformed output downstream instead of enforcing the right shape upstream; this option is the same pattern applied to execution mode — patching Batch's missing capability with a bolted-on synchronous call instead of simply running the whole analysis synchronously from the start.

stem: An agent-driven pipeline at a 500-engineer, regulated financial-services firm must have a specific tool call stopped before it ever executes, with no exceptions regardless of prompt wording. Select two mechanisms that stop the call before execution.

opts.t: A hook that logs every invocation of that tool call for later audit review.
An allow rule enumerating every other tool the agent is permitted to use, leaving this one out.
A PreToolUse hook configured to block that specific tool call.
A deny rule in the permissions settings that matches that tool call.

whyRight: Both act before the call executes: a PreToolUse hook blocks it directly, and a deny permission rule is enforced by Claude Code outside the model's discretion. Either independently satisfies 'stopped before it executes, no exceptions'; a log recorded afterward or an incomplete allow-list does not.

whyWrong.A: This creates an audit trail but does not stop the call; the decision table's own contrast is explicit — both preventive mechanisms act before execution, a log acts after.
whyWrong.B: An allow-list narrows the default path but does not stop a matching call the way an explicit deny does, and it breaks any legitimate command nobody enumerated.

t1Clause: must have a specific tool call stopped before it ever executes, with no exceptions regardless of prompt wording

deepDive.principle: Permission rules and hooks are Claude Code's deterministic enforcement layer: a deny rule is enforced by Claude Code outside the model's discretion, and a PreToolUse hook can block a call before it runs. Both act before execution. A log, an allow-list, or CLAUDE.md prose can describe or narrow behaviour, but none of them stops a specific call the way these two do.
deepDive.rightDeep: Section 7.8's row for a call that must be stopped before it executes lists two valid answers: a PreToolUse hook, or a deny permission rule — both act before execution, while a log acts after. The stem's requirement that the tool call never execute, regardless of prompt wording, is exactly that situation, and either mechanism independently satisfies it because both intervene before the call runs rather than after.

wrongDeep.A: Change the requirement from stopping the call to guaranteeing an audit entry every time it runs and this becomes a different row: an action that must happen every time a tool runs, such as an audit entry, correctly answered by a hook on the relevant event, scoped by matcher. Blocking and always-logging are different requirements answered by different placements of the same mechanism family.
wrongDeep.B: This is the corpus's own documented failure for this family: an allow-list enumerating every permitted tool narrows the default path but does not stop a matching call the way an explicit deny does, and it silently breaks any legitimate command nobody thought to enumerate — the opposite of a rule that must hold with no exceptions.

stem: A code-review check runs on every pull request at a 90-person org and must complete before the request can merge; a developer waits on the result before continuing other work. Which execution mode should the check use?

opts.t: Synchronous execution, so the result returns within the same request the developer is waiting on.
Batch API, deferring the check since batching costs fifty percent less than running it live.
Batch API, but poll for completion every few minutes so the developer learns as soon as it is ready.
Structured JSON output enforced by a schema, so the pipeline can parse results without a human reading them.

whyRight: The check gates the merge and a developer is actively waiting on its result, matching the row for a blocking pre-merge check: synchronous execution, because a developer is waiting on it. Nothing about cost or output format changes whether the result must return within this request.

whyWrong.B: The 'no fixed deadline' framing does not apply here — the stem already states a developer is waiting on the result before continuing, which Batch's unbounded up-to-24-hour window cannot satisfy.
whyWrong.C: Polling notifies the developer sooner but does not change Batch's lack of a latency SLA; the merge still waits on a window that can run up to 24 hours.
whyWrong.D: Nothing in the requirement asks for automated downstream parsing; the check only needs to finish before merge while a developer reads the result directly.

t1Clause: must complete before the request can merge; a developer waits on the result before continuing other work

deepDive.principle: Section 7.5's execution-mode choice turns on who or what is waiting on the result: a person reading and blocked on the outcome needs a bounded, live response, while Batch trades a flexible deadline for a fixed limitation — no latency SLA and up to 24 hours to return. The discriminator is whether anything is blocked, not the job's cost or its output format.
deepDive.rightDeep: The decision table's row for this shape is a blocking pre-merge check, answered synchronous, because a developer is waiting on it. The stem states the check must complete before the pull request can merge and that a developer waits on the result before continuing other work — both facts are the blocking signal that fires this row, independent of the org's size or the check's cost.

wrongDeep.B: Delete the blocking clause and this becomes the neighbouring row: an overnight report nobody is blocked on, correctly answered by Batch API for its 50% cost saving and flexible up-to-24-hour deadline. The stem instead states a developer is waiting on the result before continuing other work, which is exactly the blocking fact that row does not have.
wrongDeep.C: Batch API's own stated limitation is 'up to 24 hours, no latency SLA' — a property of the mechanism itself, not of whether someone is watching for completion. Polling changes when the developer learns the result, not how quickly Batch is obligated to produce it, so the blocking requirement remains unmet.
wrongDeep.D: This is the correct mechanism for a different requirement: findings that must be posted as inline PR comments (path, line, severity, fix) for a downstream script to parse, where JSON output with a schema guarantees a parseable shape every run. Nothing in this stem asks for automated downstream consumption — a developer reads the result directly.
